sections.title: Entra ID as the cloud identity provider
points: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) is a cloud-based identity and access management service. It needs no domain controllers on Azure virtual machines.
It is the built-in authentication and authorization service for Azure, Microsoft 365 and other SaaS apps; applications request security tokens from it.
Create and manage users in Microsoft Entra ID (Azure portal > Microsoft Entra ID > Users), not in Subscriptions, Resource groups or Virtual machines.
A user can hold several licenses, for example Microsoft 365 plus other Microsoft cloud services. Licensing is not limited to one per user.
Identities from third-party providers or on-premises AD can be trusted through federation, so access to Azure is not limited to cloud-only accounts.

sections.title: Syncing on-premises AD to Entra ID
points: Microsoft Entra Connect (Entra Connect Sync) synchronizes identities from on-premises Active Directory to Microsoft Entra ID.
To keep users working after moving resources to Azure and retiring the datacenter, sync the existing AD accounts (and optionally password hashes) to Entra ID.
Synced users keep their existing credentials, so impact on users is minimal. No re-creation or password reset is needed.
MFA adds sign-in security but does not create identities in the cloud. Guest accounts are for external users, not for migrating your own staff.

sections.title: Devices, groups and SSO in Entra ID
points: Windows 10/11 devices can be Microsoft Entra joined (or hybrid joined) so users sign in with Entra credentials; iOS and Android devices can be registered.
Group Policy is an on-premises Active Directory feature; you cannot create Group Policy objects in Microsoft Entra ID (device management uses Intune).
Groups in Entra ID support dynamic membership rules that add or remove members automatically from user or device attributes.
Users are organized with groups and administrative units. Resource groups organize Azure resources, not users.
Entra ID provides single sign-on (SSO) and can manage access to on-premises apps (for example through Application Proxy).

sections.title: Analyzing Entra security events with Sentinel
points: Microsoft Sentinel is a cloud-native SIEM/SOAR that collects and analyzes security events, including Entra ID sign-in and audit logs, through data connectors.
Microsoft Entra Connect only synchronizes identities. Key Vault stores secrets. Synapse Analytics is an analytics service, not a security-event service.

sections.title: Authentication versus authorization
points: Authentication proves identity: verifying credentials of a user or service. Authorization decides what an authenticated identity is allowed to access.
Federation, synchronization and ticketing are different concepts; Conditional Access evaluates sign-in signals to allow or deny access.
SSO lets users sign in once with one set of credentials for several apps. It does not require the Microsoft Authenticator app.
MFA requires more than one verification element (for example password plus a phone prompt) to identify a user.

sections.title: Single sign-on with Entra ID
points: Microsoft Entra ID enables SSO to many cloud and on-premises applications with a single set of credentials.
Key Vault stores secrets, application security groups group VMs for network rules, and Defender for Cloud assesses security posture. None provide SSO.

sections.title: How multi-factor authentication works
points: MFA combines factors from categories: something you know (password), something you have (phone, security key), something you are (biometric).
Valid verification methods include Microsoft Authenticator, SMS, voice call and hardware tokens. Photo ID and passport numbers are not methods.
MFA works in cloud-only environments. It does not require syncing on-premises identities or deploying federation.
MFA can be required for administrators only or for any user account.

sections.title: Password, MFA and passwordless compared
points: Password only: low security, convenient. It is the weakest option.
MFA: high security but adds steps, so less convenient.
Passwordless (Windows Hello for Business, Microsoft Authenticator, FIDO2 security keys): high security and convenient, with no password to steal.

sections.title: Microsoft Entra External ID basics
points: External identities let people outside your organization (partners, vendors, customers) access your apps and resources using their own identities.
B2B collaboration: invite external users as guests who sign in with their own organizational or social identity.
B2C / customer identity: provide sign-up and sign-in for consumer-facing apps, separate from the workforce directory.

sections.title: Conditional Access evaluates sign-in signals
points: Conditional Access is the Microsoft Entra policy engine that combines signals (user, location, device, application, risk) to make access decisions.
Decisions include block access, grant access, or grant with requirements such as MFA or a compliant device.
To limit access to apps to users whose devices meet requirements (such as being compliant or patched), create a Conditional Access policy.
Azure Firewall, Bastion and Azure Policy do not make sign-in decisions for Entra-integrated applications; managed identities and Intune are not signal engines.

sections.title: Identity Protection, PIM and Defender for Identity
points: Entra ID Protection detects risky sign-ins (such as anonymous IP addresses) and drives risk-based policies: require MFA or force a password change.
Privileged Identity Management (PIM) manages just-in-time, time-bound and approved elevation of privileged roles. It does not react to risky sign-ins.
Microsoft Defender for Identity (formerly Azure ATP) uses sensors installed on on-premises domain controllers to detect threats and compromised identities.
Microsoft Entra Connect Health monitors the health of the sync infrastructure, not sign-in risk.

sections.title: Scope and assigning Azure roles
points: Azure RBAC scopes: management group, subscription, resource group, resource. Assignments at a parent scope are inherited by child scopes.
To give a user permissions on many VMs at once, place them in the same resource group and assign the role at the resource group.
Assign roles from Access control (IAM) on the chosen scope (management group, subscription, resource group or resource).
RBAC roles also grant permissions to services such as Azure Virtual Desktop. Tags, resource groups and application security groups do not grant permissions.

sections.title: Roles and role assignments
points: Azure has built-in roles (Owner, Contributor, Reader) and supports custom roles when built-in ones don't fit.
A user can have multiple role assignments, and a scope such as a resource group can have the Owner role assigned to multiple users.

sections.title: Identity sources and federation
points: Access to Azure resources is not limited to Entra ID accounts: federation allows identities from on-premises AD or other providers to be used.
Azure has built-in authentication (Entra ID) and authorization (RBAC) services.

sections.title: Network isolation is not RBAC
points: Azure routes traffic automatically between subnets in a virtual network, so all VMs in one virtual network can communicate by default.
To prevent a VM from connecting to others, deploy it to a separate virtual network (or restrict traffic with NSGs).
Resource group, OS and number of NICs do not isolate network traffic; resource groups are logical containers for management.

sections.title: Zero Trust principles
points: Zero Trust assumes no implicit trust based on network location. Every access request is authenticated, authorized and encrypted.
Verify explicitly: use all available signals such as identity, location, device health and data classification.
Use least privilege access: limit access with just-in-time and just-enough access and risk-based adaptive policies.
Assume breach: minimize blast radius with segmentation, end-to-end encryption, and use analytics to detect threats.

sections.title: Defense-in-depth layers
points: Layers from outside in: physical security, identity and access, perimeter, network, compute, application, data.
Physical security: surveillance cameras and datacenter access controls. Identity and access: MFA, conditional access, SSO.
Perimeter: DDoS protection and firewalls at the network edge. Network: segmentation and NSGs. Compute: patching and endpoint protection.
Application: secure code and secrets management. Data: encryption of stored and transmitted data.

sections.title: Azure Key Vault for secrets and certificates
points: Azure Key Vault securely stores and controls access to secrets, keys, and certificates (passwords, API keys, connection strings, TLS certificates).
Use it to avoid exposing administrative credentials in automated deployment scripts; applications and servers retrieve secrets at runtime.
Information Protection labels documents and email; MFA verifies identity; Defender for Cloud assesses posture. None store certificates or secrets.
Storage accounts are not designed for secure secret management.

sections.title: Azure Disk Encryption prerequisite
points: Azure Disk Encryption uses BitLocker (Windows) or DM-Crypt (Linux) and stores encryption keys and secrets in Azure Key Vault.
Create the Key Vault before enabling disk encryption on the VM.

sections.title: Network filtering versus encryption
points: Azure Firewall and network security groups filter traffic by rules. They do not encrypt traffic.
Encryption in transit comes from protocols such as TLS/HTTPS or IPsec VPN, which VMs can use.
To make a VM reachable over HTTP, allow inbound port 80 (for example with an NSG rule). A DDoS protection plan only mitigates attacks, it does not open access.

sections.title: Defender for Cloud posture and compliance
points: Microsoft Defender for Cloud (formerly Security Center and Azure Defender) is a cloud security posture management (CSPM) and workload protection (CWP) platform.
It shows secure score, security recommendations, and a regulatory compliance dashboard with downloadable reports.
It monitors Azure resources and also on-premises and multicloud resources.
Basic features such as continuous assessment, recommendations and secure score are free; enhanced security features (Defender plans) are paid.

sections.title: Just-in-time VM access
points: Just-in-time (JIT) VM access, a Defender for Cloud feature, locks down inbound management ports (such as RDP and SSH) on VMs.
Access is opened temporarily on request for a limited time, reducing attack surface.
Bastion provides browser-based RDP/SSH, Firewall filters traffic, Front Door is a web delivery service. They are not the JIT feature.

sections.title: Microsoft Sentinel as SIEM
points: Microsoft Sentinel is a cloud-native SIEM (security information and event management) and SOAR (security orchestration, automation and response) solution.
Data connectors collect logs from Azure, Microsoft 365, Entra ID and VMs (such as Windows firewall logs). Data lands in a Log Analytics workspace.
It analyzes events with analytics rules, creates incidents, and can remediate automatically using automation rules and playbooks.
Azure Analysis Services, Cognitive Services and Information Protection are not SIEM solutions.

sections.title: Automating response with Sentinel playbooks
points: Playbooks are Azure Logic Apps workflows that run in response to alerts or incidents to automate and orchestrate threat response.
They are attached to analytics rules or automation rules and can run automatically.
Workbooks visualize collected data; they do not respond to threats. Adaptive network hardening and adaptive application controls belong to Defender for Cloud.

sections.title: Matching security services to tasks
points: Sentinel: SIEM, analyze security logs. Defender for Cloud: secure score, recommendations, compliance. Key Vault: store secrets, keys, certificates.
Microsoft Entra ID: identity and sign-in. Azure Lighthouse: cross-tenant management for service providers.

sections.title: Azure Firewall scope
points: Azure Firewall is a managed, stateful firewall as a service with central policies and logging across multiple subscriptions and virtual networks.
NSGs and application security groups filter at the subnet/NIC level within one virtual network scope. DDoS Protection mitigates volumetric attacks.

sections.title: What influences the cost of a resource
points: Cost factors: resource type and size, service tier, Azure region, and usage. Prices differ between regions for the same service.
Outbound data volume affects cost; the type of processed data does not. Inbound transfer does not add cost.
Storage: the price varies by region, and read/write operations and cross-region transfers are billable in general-purpose v2 accounts.
A reservation commits to a resource for a term for a discount; it does not reserve capacity at a specific datacenter.
An Azure SQL Database cannot be stopped to save money; scale the tier or use serverless auto-pause.

sections.title: Bandwidth: inbound versus outbound
points: Inbound data transfer (ingress) to Azure is free, including over VPN and ExpressRoute.
Outbound data transfer (egress) from Azure to on-premises or the internet is billed and its price varies by region.
Data transfer between services in the same region is not charged; transfers between regions are billed for the source's outbound traffic.
Resource groups are logical containers and incur no cost.

sections.title: Virtual machine billing and cost flexibility
points: Stopped (Deallocated) VMs aren't billed for compute, but disks (OS and data) and other resources like public IPs continue to incur charges.
A VM stopped from inside the guest OS stays allocated and is still billed. Stop (deallocate) it from the portal to stop compute charges.
Two VMs of the same size do not always cost the same: disks, region, OS, licensing and usage time all differ.
Reservations and savings plans lower VM cost versus pay-as-you-go. The cloud shifts spending from CapEx to OpEx and allows a mix.

sections.title: Reservations and Azure Hybrid Benefit
points: Azure Reservations are available for one-year or three-year terms. Three years is the longest term for reserved VM instances and gives the highest discount.
Azure Hybrid Benefit lets you use existing Windows Server and SQL Server licenses with Software Assurance (or subscriptions) on Azure to reduce licensing cost.
Deallocating VMs or setting budgets doesn't reduce license cost. Budgets only alert; reservations discount compute rather than licenses.

sections.title: Azure free account limits
points: A free account gives $200 credit for the first 30 days plus limited quantities of certain services free for 12 months.
Only a subset of services and tiers are included. Credit or free quantities expire, after which pay-as-you-go rates apply.
Limits apply per service (for example 5 GB blob storage), so unlimited web apps or 2 TB uploads are not included.
Free accounts are limited per person and not repeatable on the same Microsoft account.

sections.title: Agreements and Marketplace pricing
points: An Enterprise Agreement (EA) requires a predetermined (commitment) spend. Outbound traffic cost differs by region.
Third-party Marketplace offerings are priced by the publisher, not by Microsoft.

sections.title: Idle resources that do and don't cost
points: Public IP addresses (standard SKU) are billed, so deleting unused ones reduces cost.
Network interfaces, Microsoft Entra users and groups, and resource groups are not billed. Deleting them does not reduce cost.

sections.title: TCO calculator
points: The Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) calculator compares the cost of running workloads on-premises with running them in Azure.
It includes datacenter costs such as hardware, electricity, space, and IT labor, so it can show savings from reduced power use after migrating.
It produces shareable reports with graphs and is available to anyone, with no Azure account required.

sections.title: Pricing calculator versus TCO
points: The Azure pricing calculator estimates the monthly cost of Azure services you configure (region, size, tier, usage), for new deployments.
Azure Migrate assesses servers for migration readiness and sizing; Database Migration Assistant checks SQL compatibility; neither estimates power savings.

sections.title: Cost analysis in Cost Management
points: Cost Management is available to anyone with access to a billing account, subscription, resource group or management group, including pay-as-you-go.
Cost analysis views costs by scope (management group, subscription, resource group) and usage over time, such as the last three months.
No Enterprise Agreement or Software Assurance is required.

sections.title: Budgets and cost alerts
points: Budgets in Cost Management track spend against a threshold and send email alerts when actual or forecasted cost reaches a percentage.
Budgets only alert; they do not stop resources. Advisor recommendations and IAM do not send cost-limit alerts.
Tags help categorize costs but a budget is what tracks cost against a limit.

sections.title: Reducing cost of idle resources
points: Delete unused public IP addresses, which are billed. Unused user accounts, groups and network interfaces are not billed.
Azure Advisor cost recommendations identify idle resources.

sections.title: Stopping virtual machines to save cost
points: Stop a VM from the Azure portal (or CLI) so it is deallocated and compute billing stops.
Shutting down or disconnecting from inside the guest OS leaves the VM allocated and still billed.

sections.title: Tags for cost reporting and accountability
points: Tags are key-value metadata (for example Department = Finance) applied to resources, resource groups and subscriptions.
Cost reports can be grouped and filtered by tag, so you can report cost per department, office or cost center and track budgets.
Locks, policies and templates do not group costs; tags do. Budgets and alerts do not identify who owns a resource.

sections.title: Tag rules and limits
points: A resource can have multiple tags (up to 50 tag name-value pairs on most resources).
Resources do not inherit tags from the resource group or subscription; use Azure Policy to apply or inherit tags.
Tags can be applied through ARM templates. Tags are metadata and do not enforce naming standards; Azure Policy does that.

sections.title: Trust Center and Service Trust Portal
points: Microsoft Trust Center is a public site on security, privacy, compliance offerings and policies across Microsoft cloud products. No subscription needed.
Use it to check whether Azure complies with your regional or industry requirements. It is not part of Defender for Cloud.
The Service Trust Portal publishes audit reports, whitepapers and compliance resources for Microsoft cloud services.
Sign in with a Microsoft cloud services account to reach some content; My Library saves documents in one place.

sections.title: Compliance Manager
points: Purview Compliance Manager tracks regulatory compliance for Microsoft cloud services with pre-built assessments, improvement actions and a compliance score.
It is opened from the Microsoft Purview portal (formerly Microsoft 365 compliance center) using an admin account.
Defender for Cloud also has a regulatory compliance dashboard for evaluating Azure resources against standards such as ISO 27001.
Cloud Shell, Azure Advisor, Service Health and Knowledge Center do not track regulatory standards.

sections.title: Microsoft privacy and data protection documents
points: Microsoft Privacy Statement: which personal data Microsoft collects, how it is processed, and for what purpose.
Online Services Terms (now the Product Terms and Data Protection Addendum): the contractual commitments for online services.
Data Protection Addendum: data processing and security terms, including processing, transfer, retention and deletion of customer data.

sections.title: Compliance standards and regulations
points: ISO: international standards body across all industries. NIST: US standards institute used by the US government.
GDPR: EU data privacy regulation; applies to organizations offering goods or services to people in the EU. Azure can host GDPR-compliant solutions.
Azure Government: a dedicated public cloud for US federal, state and local government agencies.

sections.title: Information protection and data governance
points: Microsoft Purview Information Protection (formerly Azure Information Protection) classifies and protects documents and emails using sensitivity labels.
Labels can encrypt documents and email, and apply visual markings such as watermarks automatically when sensitive data like credit card numbers is detected.
It protects documents and emails, not network traffic, storage accounts or SQL databases.
Microsoft Purview provides data discovery and classification and data governance; it is not a backup service.

sections.title: Policy versus locks, tags and blueprints
points: Azure Policy enforces rules on resource properties, such as allowed regions or allowed VM sizes, and reports compliance.
Locks block deletion or modification; tags are metadata for organizing and cost tracking; blueprints package templates, policies and roles.
To restrict where or what resources can be created (and still allow others) use Policy. Locks and RBAC roles cannot target a resource type or region.
Management groups organize subscriptions; reservations are billing discounts.

sections.title: Policy definitions and initiatives
points: A policy definition is a single business rule that describes a compliance condition and the effect.
An initiative definition is a collection of policy definitions grouped toward one goal and assigned as a single item.

sections.title: Assigning policy and its effect
points: A policy or initiative is assigned to a scope: management group, subscription, resource group or resource.
The assignment applies to all resources within the scope; it blocks or audits non-compliant deployments depending on the effect.
Existing non-compliant resources are flagged non-compliant, not removed.

sections.title: Delete versus read-only locks
points: Two lock levels: CanNotDelete (Delete in the portal) and ReadOnly. Delete lock: authorized users can read and modify but not delete.
ReadOnly lock: users can only read, not update or delete; it is like the Reader role for everyone.
To prevent accidental deletion while allowing changes (such as creating containers), use a Delete lock; to block changes and deletes, use ReadOnly.
A ReadOnly lock still prevents deletion, but a Delete lock does not block modification.

sections.title: Lock scope and inheritance
points: Locks can be applied to subscriptions, resource groups and resources, not to users, administrative units or policies.
A lock at a parent scope is inherited by all child resources, including resources added later. The most restrictive lock wins.
A resource can have multiple locks. You can add a Delete lock to a resource that has a ReadOnly lock.
Any Azure resource can have a lock.

sections.title: Locks override user permissions
points: A lock applies to all users and roles, including owners and global administrators.
To delete a locked resource group, first remove the lock; no tag or policy change replaces that.

sections.title: Locks versus Azure Policy
points: A Policy assignment does not delete or modify existing resources. Non-compliant resources are flagged but continue to function.
Locks restrict operations on a resource; Policy governs which resources can be created and their configuration.
